definition: The exchange in which a client and server agree keys and authenticate the server (and optionally the client) before sending encrypted data.
details: TLS 1.3 needs one round trip for a full handshake, down from two in TLS 1.2, and mandates forward secrecy.
0-RTT resumption sends early data that can be replayed, so allow it only for idempotent requests.
SNI and ALPN in the ClientHello choose the certificate and the application protocol.
useCases: Configuring TLS policies at load balancers and CDNs.

definition: TLS in which both client and server present certificates, so each side authenticates the other.
details: Common for service-to-service authentication, often automated by a service mesh with short-lived certificates.
Workload identities often follow the SPIFFE standard.
Encrypts and authenticates, but authorisation policies are still needed.

definition: Announcing the same IP address from many locations so that network routing sends each user to the nearest one.
details: Used by CDNs, public DNS resolvers and global load balancers.
Failover happens in the network, without waiting for DNS TTLs to expire.
Also absorbs DDoS traffic across many points of presence.

definition: Keeping a set of open, reusable connections to a destination so requests avoid the cost of new TCP and TLS handshakes.
details: Size pools by concurrency (Little's Law) and set a timeout for acquiring a connection.
Keep the client's idle timeout below the server's and the load balancer's.
In serverless functions, create clients outside the handler so connections are reused.

definition: A simple HTTP-based protocol for a server to stream events to a browser over a long-lived response, with automatic reconnection.
details: One direction only: server to client; the client uses normal requests to send data.
Works with standard HTTP infrastructure and HTTP/2 multiplexing.
Simpler than WebSockets for notifications and streaming output such as LLM tokens.
useCases: Streaming generated text to a chat UI.

definition: The browser rule that a page from one origin (scheme, host and port) cannot read data from another origin unless that origin allows it.
details: It restricts reading responses, not sending requests, which is why CSRF is possible.
app.example.com and api.example.com are different origins but the same site.
CORS and postMessage relax it safely; CORP, COOP and CSP strengthen it.
useCases: Understanding why a fetch to another origin fails.
Designing where to host a frontend and its API.

definition: A protocol in which a server tells browsers which other origins may read its responses, using Access-Control-* headers and, for non-simple requests, an OPTIONS preflight.
details: Credentialed requests need an exact allowed origin and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true.
It does not protect servers: non-browser clients ignore it.
Reflecting any Origin with credentials is a serious vulnerability.
useCases: Single-page apps calling APIs on another origin.
Public APIs used directly from browsers.

definition: A response header that tells the browser which scripts, styles, frames and connections a page may use, providing strong defence in depth against XSS.
details: A strict CSP uses per-response nonces or hashes with 'strict-dynamic' rather than host allow-lists.
frame-ancestors controls who may frame the page, preventing clickjacking.
Roll out with Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only before enforcing.
useCases: Hardening web apps against XSS and script injection.
Limiting data exfiltration by third-party scripts.

definition: A browser API, enabled through CSP, that makes dangerous DOM sinks such as innerHTML reject plain strings unless they come from a reviewed policy.
details: Turns DOM XSS prevention from code review into enforcement.
Policies typically wrap a sanitiser such as DOMPurify.
Roll out in report-only mode first, then refactor the sinks.
useCases: Large frontends with many DOM manipulation paths.
Micro-frontend platforms with code from many teams.

definition: A cookie attribute controlling whether the browser sends the cookie on cross-site requests, a key defence against CSRF.
details: Lax blocks cross-site subrequests but allows top-level navigations with safe methods.
It works at the site level, so subdomains count as same-site.
Combine with Origin or Fetch Metadata checks for complete CSRF protection.

definition: A response header telling browsers to use only HTTPS for a domain for a set period, defeating protocol downgrade and SSL-stripping attacks.
details: includeSubDomains applies it to every subdomain, so check they all support HTTPS first.
The preload list builds the policy into browsers; removal takes months.
Typical max-age is one or two years.

definition: An integrity attribute on script and link tags containing a hash of the expected file, so the browser refuses a file that has been modified.
details: Protects against compromised CDNs or third-party hosts.
Only works for static, versioned files whose content doesn't change.
Requires crossorigin for cross-origin resources.
useCases: Micro-frontend manifests with known bundle hashes.

definition: A search data structure mapping each term to the list of documents, and positions, that contain it.
details: Queries look up only the postings lists for their terms instead of scanning documents.
Built from analysed text, so analysis decides what can be found.
Lucene stores it in immutable segments that merge over time.
useCases: PostgreSQL GIN indexes for full-text search.

definition: The standard text relevance scoring function in Lucene-based engines, combining saturating term frequency, inverse document frequency and length normalisation.
details: k1 controls term-frequency saturation and b controls length normalisation.
Rare terms count more than common ones.
Usually a baseline combined with boosts, business signals and vector similarity.
useCases: Keyword half of hybrid retrieval for RAG.

definition: The pipeline that turns raw text into index terms: character filtering, tokenising, lowercasing, stemming, synonyms and n-grams.
details: The same or compatible analysis must apply at index and query time.
Aggressive stemming and synonyms raise recall but can hurt precision.
Changing an analyser for existing data requires a reindex.
useCases: Matching users' vocabulary to catalogue terms.

definition: A method for merging ranked lists from different retrievers by summing 1 / (k + rank) for each document, avoiding the need to normalise scores.
details: k is commonly around 60.
Used to combine keyword (BM25) and vector search in hybrid retrieval.
Often followed by a cross-encoder re-ranker on the top results.

definition: An offline search relevance metric that rewards highly relevant results near the top of the list, normalised against the ideal ordering.
details: Uses graded relevance judgements for each query's results.
MRR, a simpler alternative, measures only the position of the first relevant result.
Run on a judged query set for every ranking change.
useCases: Evaluating relevance changes before A/B testing.

definition: A stable name pointing at one or more concrete search indexes, letting applications switch indexes atomically.
details: Enables zero-downtime reindexing: build a new index, then move the alias.
Keep the old index briefly for rollback.
Filtered aliases can scope queries, for example per tenant.
useCases: Re-embedding documents with a new model.

definition: Serving many customers (tenants) from one software system, with isolation choices per layer: silo (dedicated), pool (shared) or bridge (a mix).
details: Choose isolation per layer and per tier, usually pooled by default and siloed where needed.
Tenant context must flow through requests, events, jobs, logs and caches.
Noisy neighbours and cross-tenant leaks are the main pooled-model risks.

definition: A database feature that filters rows according to a policy, such as matching a tenant id in the session, so isolation is enforced by the database rather than by every query.
details: In PostgreSQL, use FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY so table owners are also subject to policies.
Set the tenant per transaction (set_config with is_local true) to stay safe with connection pools.
Roles with BYPASSRLS or superuser rights skip policies, so the application must not use them.

definition: A tenant or workload that consumes so much of a shared resource that others' performance suffers.
details: Mitigate with per-tenant rate limits and quotas, fair queues and separate pools for heavy work.
Per-tenant usage visibility shows who the neighbours are.
Outsized tenants may need to move to dedicated capacity or their own cell.
useCases: Pooled SaaS databases and job queues.

definition: The part of a system that manages configuration and lifecycle (in SaaS: tenants, tiers, onboarding, billing), as opposed to the plane that serves the actual workload.
details: In SaaS, the application plane reads tenant context and entitlements from the control plane.
Data planes should keep working on cached configuration if the control plane is unavailable.
Control planes are usually more complex and less available than data planes.
useCases: Tenant onboarding and routing in SaaS.
Cloud provider and Kubernetes architecture discussions.

definition: Splitting a system into multiple identical, independent copies (cells or stamps), each serving a subset of customers, to limit the blast radius of failures and scale by adding cells.
details: A routing layer maps each tenant or customer to its cell.
Cells are sized by blast-radius tolerance and tested capacity.
Requires tenant placement and migration tooling for rebalancing.

definition: The features, limits and isolation level a tenant is allowed under its plan or contract, stored as data and checked through a single service.
details: Keep commercial entitlements separate from temporary release feature flags.
Enforce on the server, not just by hiding UI.
Usage metering shows tenants their consumption and feeds billing.
useCases: Free, standard and enterprise SaaS tiers.

definition: Any information relating to an identified or identifiable living person, including online identifiers such as IP addresses and cookie ids.
details: Special category data (health, biometrics, ethnicity, religion and others) needs extra conditions and protection.
Combinations of ordinary attributes can identify someone.
The US term PII is often narrower than GDPR's definition.
useCases: Deciding what can be logged or shared with vendors.

definition: Replacing direct identifiers with tokens or keys held separately; unlike anonymisation, the data remains personal data under GDPR.
details: Reduces risk and is encouraged by GDPR, but re-identification remains possible.
True anonymisation must make re-identification not reasonably possible, which is hard.
A hashed email is a pseudonym, not anonymous data.

definition: The GDPR principle of collecting, keeping and sharing only the personal data needed for a specific purpose.
details: Question every field in forms, APIs and logs.
Store derived values (an age band, a verification result) instead of raw data where possible.
Reduces breach impact, storage and the work of subject requests.
useCases: Deciding what to send to analytics vendors.

definition: One of the six GDPR grounds that make processing personal data lawful: consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task or legitimate interests.
details: Consent is wrong for processing the service can't work without; use contract instead.
Legitimate interests needs a balancing test and an opt-out.
Record the basis per purpose in the data inventory.
useCases: Designing a new feature that uses personal data.
Reusing data for a new purpose such as model training.

definition: A request from a person exercising their privacy rights, such as access, correction, erasure or portability, which must be answered within legal deadlines.
details: Under GDPR, the default deadline is one month, extendable by two months for complex requests.
Verify the requester's identity before releasing data.
Automate with a central workflow and export and erase handlers in each service.

definition: The GDPR right (Article 17) for people to have their personal data deleted when there is no longer a valid reason to keep it.
details: Exceptions include legal retention obligations such as invoices.
Deletion must cover derived copies, vendors and, by some means, backups.
Records kept for aggregates can be anonymised instead of deleted.

definition: Erasing data by encrypting it with a dedicated key (per person or tenant) and destroying the key, making every copy unreadable.
details: The standard approach for erasure from immutable event logs and backups.
Needs a highly available key management service and short key caching.
Consumers must handle events whose key no longer exists.

definition: An assessment required by GDPR before processing likely to result in high risk to people, describing the processing, its necessity, the risks and the mitigations.
details: Triggers include large-scale special category data, systematic monitoring, profiling and new technologies such as AI.
Engineers contribute data flows and technical mitigations.
Best done during design and updated as the design changes.
useCases: Launching AI features using customer data.

definition: Requirements, from law, regulation or contract, that data is stored and processed in specific geographic locations.
details: Covers backups, logs, telemetry, support access and vendors, not just the main database.
Often met with regional deployment stamps and a minimal global control plane.
GDPR permits transfers with safeguards, so many residency demands are contractual.
useCases: Public sector and financial services workloads.

definition: A mathematical guarantee that the output of an analysis changes very little whether or not any one person's data is included, achieved by adding calibrated noise.
details: The privacy budget (epsilon) trades accuracy against privacy.
Used by the US Census Bureau and in large-scale telemetry.
Needs expertise to apply correctly.

definition: A description of the load a performance test reproduces: operation mix, arrival rates, user behaviour, data variety and payloads, ideally derived from production data.
details: A test is only as useful as its workload model.
Include spike shapes, bots and client retry behaviour for launches.
Refresh it as usage changes.
useCases: Planning load tests for a launch.

definition: Two ways of generating load: open models send requests at a fixed arrival rate regardless of response time; closed models use a fixed number of users who wait for each response.
details: Closed models reduce load as the system slows, hiding overload.
Open models reproduce real internet traffic, where requests pile up when the system slows.
In k6, use constant-arrival-rate or ramping-arrival-rate executors for open models.
useCases: Modelling a fixed pool of batch workers (closed).

definition: A measurement error where a load generator waits for slow responses before sending more requests, so it under-records the latency real users would see during stalls.
details: Named by Gil Tene.
Avoid with open-model generators that measure from the intended send time.
Cross-check client results with server-side and real-user latency.

definition: Brendan Gregg's method for finding bottlenecks: for every resource, check utilisation, saturation (queued work) and errors.
details: Covers CPU, memory, disks, network, pools, queues and locks.
The first saturated resource usually explains rising latency.
Complements the RED method for request-driven services.
useCases: Diagnosing a load test that fails at a certain throughput.

definition: Neil Gunther's model of how throughput scales with load or nodes, accounting for contention (serialised work) and coherency (coordination) costs.
details: Explains why throughput flattens and can even fall as nodes are added.
Fit it to measured throughput at several instance counts to predict limits.
Amdahl's law is the special case with contention only.
useCases: Deciding whether scaling out will help.
Capacity planning for shared stateful resources.

definition: The combination that makes prompt injection dangerous for an AI agent: access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and a way to communicate externally.
details: Any text the agent reads can carry instructions, so assume injection will sometimes succeed.
Remove at least one leg per task: no secrets, no untrusted input, or no egress.
Enforce this in the harness (permissions, sandbox, network policy), not in the prompt.
useCases: Threat-modelling a coding agent that browses the web.
Deciding which tools an email-triage agent may hold.

definition: Registering package names that AI coding tools tend to hallucinate, so that developers who install the suggested dependency get the attacker's code.
details: A variant of typosquatting driven by model hallucinations rather than human typos.
Mitigate with dependency allow-lists, registry proxies and CI checks on package age and existence.
useCases: Justifying a CI check on newly added dependencies.

definition: A model that scores a query and a candidate document together, giving more precise relevance than embedding similarity, at the cost of running once per pair.
details: Embedding models (bi-encoders) give recall over the whole corpus; rerankers give precision over the top 50–100 candidates.
Adds tens to hundreds of milliseconds, so cap the candidate count.
useCases: Improving RAG answer quality without changing the index.
Ordering search results after hybrid retrieval.

definition: How well a model's predicted probabilities match observed frequencies: of cases scored 0.2, about 20% should be positive.
details: A model can rank well (high AUC) and still be badly calibrated.
Check with reliability diagrams or the Brier score; fix with Platt scaling or isotonic regression on held-out data.
Resampling and class weights distort probabilities, so recalibrate after using them.
useCases: Expected-cost thresholds for fraud or credit decisions.
Comparing or combining scores across models and segments.

definition: Predicting the change in an outcome caused by an action (contacting a customer, giving a discount), rather than the outcome itself.
details: Needs randomised experiment data with treated and control groups.
Targets 'persuadables' and avoids spending on sure things, lost causes and people the action annoys.
useCases: Marketing offers with a limited budget.

definition: A shared service between applications and model providers that handles auth, routing, fallbacks, budgets, logging and safety filters for LLM calls.
details: Model aliases ("default-fast") let the platform swap concrete model versions without code changes.
Attributes every request's token cost to a team and feature.
Should stay thin: product teams keep ownership of their prompts and evals.
useCases: Cost control and observability across many teams.
Migrating off a deprecated model version.

definition: A screening heuristic from US employment guidance: a group's selection rate below 80% of the highest group's rate suggests adverse impact worth investigating.
details: It's a screen, not a legal safe harbour or proof of discrimination.
Measures demographic parity only; check error-rate metrics too.
useCases: Auditing a CV-screening or promotion model.

definition: RPO is the maximum acceptable data loss, measured in time; RTO is the maximum acceptable time to restore service after a disruption.
details: They drive the disaster-recovery tier: backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby or active-active.
Only tested restores and failover drills tell you your real RPO and RTO.
useCases: Setting DR requirements for a database.
Comparing the cost of DR options in an ADR.

definition: A consumer records each processed message id in the same transaction as its own state change, so redelivered messages are detected and skipped.
details: The partner of the transactional outbox: the outbox gives at-least-once delivery, the inbox makes it effectively-once.
Prune ids older than the broker's maximum redelivery window.
useCases: Billing reacting to OrderPaid events without double-invoicing.

definition: An infrastructure layer that handles service-to-service (east–west) traffic: mutual TLS, retries, timeouts, traffic splitting and telemetry, without application code changes.
details: Implemented with sidecar proxies or, in newer designs, node-level (sidecar-less) proxies.
A significant operational investment; justified at real service counts or with zero-trust requirements.
Keep business logic out of it, as with an API gateway.
useCases: Canary releases by percentage of traffic.

definition: A service that stores versioned event or message schemas and enforces compatibility rules when producers register new versions.
details: Compatibility modes include backward, forward and full.
Fails a breaking change at publish time or in CI, rather than in a consumer at runtime.
useCases: Evolving a Kafka event that many teams consume.

definition: A pattern that tracks the changes made during one business operation and commits them together in a single transaction.
details: ORMs such as Entity Framework and Hibernate already implement it, together with repositories.
Wrapping an ORM in another generic unit of work usually adds layers without benefit.
useCases: Saving an aggregate and its outbox row atomically.

definition: A free template for architecture documentation with 12 sections, from goals and constraints through views, decisions and quality requirements to risks and a glossary.
details: Meant to be used selectively: fill in only the sections that help.
C4 diagrams fit its context, building-block and deployment views; ADRs fit its decisions section.
useCases: Structuring the docs/architecture folder of a new system.

definition: A protocol that commits one transaction across several participants: a prepare phase in which each participant votes, then a commit or abort decided and announced by a coordinator.
details: A participant that votes yes must wait for the decision while holding its locks, so a coordinator crash leaves it in doubt (blocking).
Spanner runs 2PC across Paxos-replicated groups so a failed coordinator doesn't block participants.
useCases: Atomic commits across shards inside one distributed database.
Explaining why cross-service workflows use sagas instead.

definition: A timestamp made of a physical time component and a logical counter. It respects causality like a Lamport clock while staying close to wall-clock time.
details: On receipt, wall = max(local, remote, physical); the counter breaks ties and resets once physical time moves ahead.
CockroachDB and YugabyteDB use HLCs with a configured maximum clock offset.
useCases: Ordering multi-version writes in a distributed database.
Time-range queries over causally ordered events.

definition: A Raft technique for linearizable reads: the leader records its commit index, confirms it is still leader with a heartbeat round, waits until it has applied that index, then reads locally.
details: Costs one network round trip and no log write.
Followers can serve linearizable reads by fetching the read index from the leader.
useCases: Spreading read load across a Raft cluster.

definition: Running a distributed system's real code in one process against a simulated network, disk and clock driven by a seeded random generator, so any failure found can be replayed exactly.
details: Pioneered by FoundationDB, and used by TigerBeetle and the Antithesis platform.
Requires all I/O, time and randomness behind interfaces from the start.
useCases: Finding rare interleavings of crashes and message reordering in consensus or storage code.

definition: A workshop format, created by Alberto Brandolini, in which domain experts and engineers model a business process as a timeline of past-tense domain events on sticky notes.
details: Runs at big-picture, process and design levels.
Pivotal events, where responsibility hands over, suggest bounded-context boundaries.
useCases: Discovering bounded contexts in a monolith.
Building a shared ubiquitous language quickly.

definition: A domain object defined entirely by its attributes, with no identity. It is immutable, compared by value and validates itself on construction.
details: Examples: Money, EmailAddress, DateRange.
Removes primitive obsession and makes invalid values impossible to construct.
useCases: Modelling amounts with currency instead of raw numbers.

definition: A record of something significant that happened in the domain, named in the past tense (OrderPlaced), raised by an aggregate.
details: Internal to a bounded context; translate selected ones into versioned integration events for other contexts.
Used to update other aggregates with eventual consistency.
useCases: Triggering loyalty points after an order is placed.

definition: A diagram of a system's bounded contexts and the relationship between each pair: partnership, shared kernel, customer–supplier, conformist, anticorruption layer, open host service or separate ways.
details: Draw the current reality first, then the intended relationships.
The relationships reflect team dynamics as much as technology.
useCases: Planning integration and team ownership across contexts.

definition: The precise vocabulary that domain experts and developers share within one bounded context, used in conversation, tests and code alike.
details: Bounded: the same word may mean different things in different contexts.
Awkward or ambiguous language signals a modelling problem or a hidden boundary.
useCases: Naming aggregates, methods and events after business terms.

definition: A component that reacts to events and sends commands to drive a multi-step process across aggregates or contexts, keeping its own state and running compensations on failure.
details: Holds no business rules of its own; the aggregates enforce them.
An orchestrated saga is a process manager with compensations.
useCases: Reserving seats, starting a booking and taking payment as separate transactions.

definition: A complete, independent copy of an application's infrastructure, deployed per region or per group of tenants, so capacity and residency scale by adding stamps.
details: A global control plane routes each tenant to its stamp.
Closely related to cells: both limit blast radius.
useCases: Keeping EU tenants' data in an EU stamp.

definition: Recording what each tenant consumed (API calls, storage, compute) as idempotent usage events that feed rating and invoicing.
details: Deterministic event ids make retries safe to deduplicate.
Corrections are new adjustment events, never edits to history.
useCases: Showing tenants their consumption before they hit a limit.

definition: Granting elevated access only when needed, tied to a reason, approved, scoped and automatically expiring, instead of standing privileges.
details: Every grant and action is audited.
Break-glass access is a separate, alarmed path for emergencies.
useCases: Support engineers viewing one tenant's data for a ticket.
Production database access during an incident.

definition: A way to map keys to nodes by placing both on a ring of hash values, so that adding or removing a node moves only about 1/N of the keys.
details: Virtual nodes (many points per node) keep the load balanced; with one point per node, load can be very uneven.
Plain hash % N moves most keys whenever N changes.
useCases: Distributing cache keys across a changing set of nodes.

definition: A UUID version defined in RFC 9562 (2024) that starts with a 48-bit Unix millisecond timestamp followed by random bits, so ids sort roughly by creation time.
details: Needs no coordination between generators.
Keeps B-tree inserts close together, unlike random UUIDv4.
useCases: Primary keys in distributed systems and databases.

definition: A single key that receives far more traffic than its partition or cache node can serve, so adding nodes doesn't help.
details: Hot reads: local caches, replicated copies, request coalescing.
Hot writes: split into sub-keys, batch updates, or aggregate asynchronously.

definition: A queue in front of a high-demand flow that admits users at the rate the back end can sustain, turning a traffic spike into a controlled stream.
details: Positions are randomised at opening time so refreshing or bots gain nothing.
Served as static content from the edge, so waiting users cost little.

definition: Bertrand Meyer's principle that a method should either change state (a command) or return information (a query), but not both.
details: Atomic operations such as pop or compare-and-set are deliberate exceptions, because splitting them creates races.
CQRS applies the same idea at the architecture level.
useCases: Making queries safe to call in logs, assertions and retries.

definition: Building behaviour by combining small collaborating objects or functions rather than by extending base classes.
details: Avoids the fragile base class problem and the explosion of subclasses for every combination.
Inheritance still suits small, stable is-a hierarchies designed for extension.
useCases: A report job composed from any renderer and any delivery method.

definition: A structure that keeps decisions in pure functions (the core) and confines I/O, time and randomness to a thin outer layer (the shell).
details: The core is tested with plain inputs and outputs, without mocks.
Popularised by Gary Bernhardt.
useCases: Nightly jobs whose decisions must be easy to test.

definition: A place where you can change a program's behaviour without editing the code at that point, such as an injected dependency or an overridable method. Michael Feathers' term.
details: Used to get legacy code under test before refactoring it.
Constructor parameters with default values are a common, low-risk seam.
useCases: Replacing a hard-wired database call with a fake in a characterisation test.

definition: An announced, short window in which a deprecated API or feature deliberately fails, to reveal consumers that still depend on it before it is removed.
details: Callers get a clear error linking to the migration guide.
Repeated with growing duration as the removal date approaches.

definition: A program that rewrites source code automatically, usually by transforming its syntax tree, to apply the same change across many files or repositories.
details: Tools include jscodeshift and ts-morph (TypeScript), OpenRewrite (Java) and Roslyn code fixes (.NET).
Combined with bulk pull-request tooling for organisation-wide migrations.
useCases: Upgrading a framework across hundreds of services.
Replacing a deprecated library call everywhere.

definition: A standard JSON format for HTTP API errors, with type, title, status, detail and instance fields plus custom extensions.
details: Clients branch on the stable type URI, not on message text.
RFC 9457 obsoleted RFC 7807.
useCases: Consistent validation and business-rule errors across all of an organisation's APIs.

definition: Writing and reviewing the API contract (OpenAPI, Protobuf, GraphQL SDL or AsyncAPI) before implementing it, and treating it as the source of truth.
details: Mocks, clients, server stubs and validation are generated from the contract.
CI lints the contract and blocks unintended breaking changes.
useCases: Letting frontend and partner teams build against a mock while the backend is written.

definition: An API pattern for slow work: the request returns 202 Accepted with a link to an operation resource, which the client polls or is notified about when it completes.
details: Combine with an idempotency key so a retried request doesn't start a second operation.
Google AIP-151 defines the same idea for gRPC APIs.
useCases: Report generation, large exports and provisioning.

definition: An OAuth mechanism that binds an access token to a client-held key; every request carries a signed proof covering the method, URL and token, so a stolen token alone can't be used.
details: The token's cnf.jkt claim holds the key thumbprint.
Required or recommended by high-security profiles such as FAPI 2.0.
useCases: Protecting refresh tokens on mobile clients.

definition: Requiring a stronger or more recent authentication before a sensitive action, checked server-side against the token's acr, amr and auth_time claims.
details: RFC 9470 defines the insufficient_user_authentication challenge an API returns.
Combine with notifications and cooling-off periods for the riskiest changes.

definition: Issuing a new refresh token on every refresh and invalidating the old one; if an already-used token is presented again, the whole token family is revoked as stolen.
details: A short reuse interval avoids false alarms when a client retries a refresh after a dropped response.
Store only hashes of refresh tokens.
useCases: Mobile and single-page apps with long-lived sessions.

definition: A Kafka retention policy that keeps at least the latest message for each key instead of deleting by time, turning a topic into a changelog of current state.
details: A tombstone (null value) deletes a key after delete.retention.ms.
Consumers may still see some older values that haven't been compacted yet.

definition: How far a consumer group is behind the newest messages: per partition, the latest offset minus the committed offset, ideally also expressed as the age of the oldest unprocessed message.
details: Monitor per partition, so one stuck partition isn't hidden by healthy ones.
Adding consumers beyond the partition count doesn't reduce it.

definition: A timer persisted in a store so it survives restarts and can be cancelled or changed, fired by workers that poll for due entries.
details: SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED lets several schedulers poll without blocking each other.
Workflow engines such as Temporal provide durable timers built in.
useCases: Reminders at a user's local time.

definition: Keeping a product's most important functions working, with reduced features, when part of the system fails or is overloaded.
details: Decided in advance per dependency: hide, serve cached or default data, queue for later, or fail closed.
Fallbacks must be exercised regularly, or they're broken when needed.
useCases: A product page without reviews that still lets people buy.

definition: Temporarily removing individual backend instances from a load-balancing pool when their real traffic shows far more errors or latency than their peers.
details: Ejection time grows with repeated ejections.
A maximum ejection percentage stops a shared problem from emptying the pool.
useCases: Routing around one bad pod whose health endpoint still passes.

definition: A limit on in-flight requests that adjusts itself from observed latency, raising the limit while latency stays near its minimum and cutting it when queues form.
details: Modelled on TCP congestion control (Vegas, Gradient, AIMD).
Requests beyond the limit are rejected immediately.
useCases: Protecting a service from overload without hand-tuned limits.

definition: A structured review listing, for each dependency, how it can fail, the effect on users, how the failure is detected, and the mitigation.
details: Rank rows by likelihood and impact, and focus on untested mitigations.
Turn findings into timeouts, alerts, runbooks and chaos experiments.
useCases: A design review before launching a critical service.

definition: The mechanism by which a sender learns the largest packet size a route can carry, using ICMP 'fragmentation needed' or 'packet too big' messages.
details: Blocking those ICMP messages creates a black hole: small packets work, large ones vanish.
MSS clamping on tunnel routers is the common fix.
useCases: Diagnosing connections that hang after the TLS handshake over a VPN.

definition: TCP's start-up behaviour: a new connection begins with a small congestion window (commonly about 14 KB) and roughly doubles it each round trip.
details: Large responses on new connections need several round trips regardless of bandwidth.
Warm, reused connections avoid paying it again.
useCases: Explaining why CDNs and connection reuse speed up first loads.

definition: A client algorithm that races IPv6 and IPv4 connection attempts and uses whichever connects first, so a broken IPv6 path doesn't add long delays.
details: Makes publishing AAAA records at the edge low-risk.
Defined in RFC 8305.
useCases: Rolling out dual-stack at a CDN or load balancer.

definition: Layered defences against distributed denial-of-service attacks: anycast absorption at the edge for volumetric floods, protocol limits in proxies, and WAF rules, rate limits and load shedding for application-layer attacks.
details: Origins should accept traffic only through the protected edge.
Runbooks and provider contacts are prepared before an attack.
useCases: Protecting a public API and its login endpoint.

definition: A garbage-collection design that splits the heap into a small, frequently collected young generation and a larger old generation for objects that survive.
details: V8 collects the young generation with the Scavenger and the old generation with mark-compact, much of it concurrently.
In containers, set the old-generation limit well below the memory limit.
useCases: Tuning Node.js memory for Kubernetes pods.

definition: A stateful, allow-only virtual firewall attached to network interfaces in an AWS VPC. Return traffic for an allowed connection is permitted automatically.
details: Rules can reference other security groups instead of IP ranges, which expresses intent and survives scaling.
Azure's closest equivalent is a network security group (NSG), which also supports deny rules.
useCases: Allowing only the load balancer's group to reach a service's port.
Restricting a database to its application's tasks.

definition: A stateless list of numbered allow and deny rules applied to all traffic entering or leaving an AWS subnet.
details: Rules are evaluated lowest number first, and the first match wins.
Being stateless, it needs explicit rules for return traffic on ephemeral ports.
useCases: Quickly blocking a known bad address range for a whole subnet.
A coarse backstop between public and data subnets.

definition: The extra latency when a serverless platform must create a new execution environment (download code, start the runtime, run initialisation) before handling a request.
details: Reduced by smaller bundles, lazy loading, snapshots such as Lambda SnapStart, and provisioned concurrency.
Lambda has billed the init phase for every configuration since August 2025.
useCases: Explaining p99 latency spikes on a user-facing Lambda API after a traffic burst.

definition: A set of preventive guardrails ensuring that only trusted identities access trusted resources from expected networks, so one misconfiguration or stolen credential can't leak data.
details: On AWS: RCPs and resource policies for identities, SCPs and VPC endpoint policies for resources, and network condition keys.
Key conditions include aws:PrincipalOrgID, aws:ResourceOrgID and aws:SourceVpce.
useCases: Blocking access to company buckets from outside the organisation, even if a bucket policy is too open.

definition: An AWS Organizations policy that caps what can be done to resources in member accounts, whoever the caller is, including principals outside the organisation.
details: Like SCPs, it only limits and never grants.
Introduced in November 2024 for S3, STS, KMS, SQS and Secrets Manager, and since extended to more services.
useCases: Denying access to any S3 bucket in the organisation from principals outside it.

definition: A Microsoft Entra identity that Azure creates and manages for a resource, so code can get tokens for other Azure services without any stored secret.
details: System-assigned identities live and die with one resource. User-assigned ones are standalone and can be shared.
Grant it least-privilege RBAC roles at the narrowest scope.
useCases: An app reading Key Vault secrets and Blob Storage with no connection strings.

definition: Letting an external workload exchange a token from its own OIDC issuer (such as GitHub Actions or a Kubernetes cluster) for short-lived cloud credentials, based on a configured trust in that issuer, subject and audience.
details: On Azure it's a federated credential on a managed identity or app registration. On AWS it's AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity with a role trust policy.
Scope the subject to a repository and environment, so only approved jobs get production access.
useCases: CI pipelines deploying to the cloud without stored keys.

definition: A network interface with a private IP in your virtual network that connects to one specific PaaS resource, so traffic to it never uses the public endpoint.
details: Needs private DNS so the service's normal hostname resolves to the private IP.
Disable public network access on the resource once it's in place.
useCases: Reaching Azure SQL, Storage and Key Vault only from the application's VNet and on-premises.

definition: Azure's managed networking service providing Microsoft-run hubs with any-to-any transit between VNets, branches, remote users and ExpressRoute across regions.
details: A secured virtual hub adds Azure Firewall, and routing intent sends traffic through it.
You can't deploy your own resources inside a virtual hub.
useCases: Connecting dozens of branch offices and several regions without hand-built routing.

definition: A managed entry point in front of APIs that applies cross-cutting policies such as authentication, rate limits, quotas, transformation, caching and analytics.
details: Examples: Azure API Management, Amazon API Gateway, Kong, Apigee.
Subscription or API keys identify consumers for quotas. They aren't authentication.
useCases: Publishing partner APIs with per-consumer quotas and JWT validation.

definition: A system that tests each pull request combined with the changes ahead of it in a queue, and merges only if that combination passes, so main stays green.
details: Batching keeps throughput high. A failed batch is split to find the culprit.
It catches semantic conflicts that per-PR checks against an old main miss.
useCases: A busy monorepo where many PRs merge every hour.

definition: Releasing a change to gradually larger slices of traffic or users while automatically comparing its health with the current version, then promoting or rolling back without waiting for a person.
details: Tools include Argo Rollouts, Flagger and cloud deployment services.
The canary needs enough requests for the comparison to be meaningful.
useCases: A 5% to 25% to 100% rollout that aborts when the error rate rises.

definition: Running the new version alongside the old one, then switching all traffic to it at once, with the old version kept ready for an instant switch back.
details: Needs double capacity during the switch.
The database schema must work with both versions.
useCases: Releasing a service where mixed versions during a rolling update would be a problem.

definition: A CI attack in which a privileged workflow, such as GitHub Actions' pull_request_target, checks out and runs code from an untrusted pull request, giving the attacker its secrets and write token.
details: Prevent it by running untrusted code only in unprivileged workflows.
Treat anything an unprivileged run produces as untrusted input.
useCases: Auditing workflows in open-source repositories that accept fork PRs.
